lines.text: Five thousand years of cities, empires, faiths and freedom. This is the story of India, from the Indus Valley to the most populous nation on Earth.
It begins on the banks of the Indus, where a Bronze Age people built planned cities with drains and standard weights, then faded without a written history.
They left behind short strings of symbols on seals and pots. No one has ever read them, and scholars still argue whether they are a language at all.
Their greatest city was Mohenjo-daro, with straight streets, brick houses and covered drains, laid out more than four thousand years ago.
Many centuries later, Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nanda kings of the north and stood up to the Greek ruler Seleucus.
The Maurya Empire he founded was the first to unite most of the subcontinent under one rule.
His grandson Ashoka pushed it further, but after a bloody war in Kalinga he turned to Buddhism and to a rule of tolerance.
At the Mauryan court, tradition places the Arthashastra, a hard-headed handbook on taxes, spies and war linked to the minister Chanakya.
Ashoka carved his ideals on rocks and pillars across his lands, urging kindness to people and animals, among the earliest writing in India anyone can read.
In the cliffs of Maharashtra, Buddhist monks began cutting the Ajanta Caves, later filled with paintings and sculpture of great beauty.
From the fourth century the Gupta Empire brought a golden age of science, art and poetry, when the great Kalidasa wrote.
At Nalanda, in today's Bihar, a great Buddhist monastery drew students from across Asia for nearly eight hundred years.
The astronomer Aryabhata gave a fine value for pi and said day and night come from the Earth turning. India's first satellite bears his name.
And in 628 Brahmagupta set out rules for zero in sums, an Indian idea that travelled through the Islamic world to Europe and made modern counting possible.
In the south the Chola kings became a sea power, sending fleets and traders to Southeast Asia and raising great temples like Thanjavur's.
In the north, from 1206, the Delhi Sultanate ruled for three centuries, building the Qutb Minar and holding back the Mongols.
Further south rose Vijayanagara, a Hindu empire whose capital at Hampi was one of the richest cities in the world.
In 1526 Babur, a descendant of Timur, came down from Kabul and defeated the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat.
So began the Mughal Empire, which would blend Persian and Indian culture and rule most of the subcontinent for generations.
Its greatest ruler, Akbar, united most of the north, ran an efficient state and welcomed the many faiths of his people.
Under Shah Jahan, Mughal art and building reached their height, though he ended his days held captive by his own son.
That son, Aurangzeb, seized the throne after a war with his brothers and ruled for nearly fifty years, fighting long wars in the Deccan.
Against him rose Shivaji in the west, who built forts and a navy, fought with speed and surprise, and was crowned in 1674.
Meanwhile at Agra stood Shah Jahan's tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, the white marble Taj Mahal, the jewel of Mughal architecture.
Shivaji's Maratha kingdom grew into an empire that controlled much of India and would fight the British in three wars.
But in 1757, at Plassey, Robert Clive and the East India Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal, and British rule in India began.
A century later, Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi led her troops in the field against the Company and died in battle, a lasting symbol of resistance.
She fought in the great rebellion of 1857, which began with soldiers in Meerut and spread across the north before it was crushed.
Afterwards the British Crown took direct control. The Raj built railways and offices, but it also saw terrible famines and a growing call for freedom.
Rabindranath Tagore, poet and teacher, became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, and wrote the anthem India sings today.
Then came Mahatma Gandhi, the lawyer who led the struggle against British rule with nonviolent protest, and changed the way the world resists.
Vallabhbhai Patel stood beside him, and after freedom brought more than five hundred princely states into the new nation.
Muhammad Ali Jinnah led the Muslim League and argued for a separate Muslim homeland, which became Pakistan.
The Indian National Congress, founded in Bombay in 1885, became the great vehicle of the freedom movement, and later governed India for many years.
From a poor family in the south, the self-taught Srinivasa Ramanujan sent his formulas to Cambridge and astonished the world before dying young.
Jawaharlal Nehru, Gandhi's close ally, would become free India's first prime minister and hold the office for seventeen years.
B. R. Ambedkar, born a Dalit, fought caste discrimination all his life and led the drafting of India's constitution.
The Muslim League, founded in Dhaka in 1906, came under Jinnah to demand a state of its own.
Nehru's daughter, Indira Gandhi, would lead India for most of the years from 1966, through war and crisis, until she was assassinated in 1984.
And Lata Mangeshkar would become the voice of Indian cinema, singing for Hindi films for more than seventy years.
In 1930 Gandhi walked for about three weeks to the sea to make salt against the British tax, and the whole world watched.
A year later Bombay's film studios made their first sound films. Bollywood's mix of romance, song and dance would win audiences far beyond India.
A. P. J. Abdul Kalam would lead India's missile programme and then, as president, be loved as the people's president.
Ratan Tata would take the Tata group abroad, buying Jaguar Land Rover and more, and give generously to education and health.
But during the Second World War, famine struck Bengal. Crop disease, wartime disruption and failed policies cost millions of lives.
In the years that followed, new high-yield crops, fertiliser and irrigation began to transform India's harvests and help keep famine away.
In August 1947 British India was divided into India and Pakistan. Millions fled across the new borders, and a great many were killed.
Out of that pain, independent India was born, a republic of many languages and faiths, and in time the most populous country on Earth.
Its constitution, one of the longest in the world, came into force in 1950, guaranteeing basic rights in a federal democracy.
Narendra Modi would rise from Gujarat to become prime minister in 2014, leading the BJP through years of sweeping reform.
Kalpana Chawla, born in India, became the first woman of Indian origin in space, and was lost with the shuttle Columbia in 2003.
In 1962 a short war in the Himalayas ended in defeat by China, a hard lesson for the young republic.
In 1969 India founded its space agency, which would launch its own satellites and reach the Moon and Mars.
In 1971 India went to war with Pakistan again. It ended in Dhaka with a Pakistani surrender and a new nation, Bangladesh.
Sachin Tendulkar would give the country its cricketing hero, scoring more international runs than anyone in history.
But in 1975 Indira Gandhi declared the Emergency, ruling by decree for twenty-one months, jailing opponents and censoring the press.
In 1984 poison gas leaked from a pesticide plant in Bhopal, one of the worst industrial disasters the world has known.
In 1991, in a deep crisis, Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh cut licences and tariffs and opened India to the world economy.
On Boxing Day 2004 a great tsunami crossed the Indian Ocean, striking India's coasts among many others.
Four years later, gunmen from Pakistan attacked a station and hotels in Mumbai, killing more than a hundred and sixty people over four days.
In 2014 India's Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on its very first try, and at a remarkably low cost.
In 2016 most of the country's cash was withdrawn overnight in a strike against untaxed money, and queues at banks lasted for weeks.
Then came the COVID pandemic, with lockdowns, a fast vaccine drive and great hardship for a country of over a billion people.
And in August 2023 Chandrayaan-3 touched down near the Moon's south pole, making India the fourth nation to land softly on the Moon.
From the Indus to the Moon, India's long story keeps unfolding.
